2611.14635.title: FRIDA: Finding Rotation In ultra-Diffuse gAlaxies. I. Programme overview, resolved gas density profiles, and HI mass-size relation

2611.14635.abstract:
Gas-rich ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) provide powerful tests of galaxy formation models at low surface densities. However, the structure of their neutral atomic hydrogen (HI) remains poorly constrained, hampering our understanding of this population.
We present FRIDA (Finding Rotation In ultra-Diffuse gAlaxies), a MeerKAT and VLA programme providing high-resolution HI data of 12 gas-rich UDGs. In this paper, we introduce our sample and delve into the associated observations and data reduction. We derive HI fluxes, masses ($M_{\rm HI}$), and resolved surface density profiles ($\Sigma_{\rm HI}(R)$). We find extended ($\sim 7-30\ \rm{kpc}$ in radius) and regular HI emission in our UDGs, and we report the discovery of a satellite around one of them. Most UDGs in FRIDA have $\Sigma_{\rm HI}(R)$ profiles with flat inner parts reaching $\Sigma_{\rm HI}(R)\approx 4\ M_\odot\ \rm{pc^{-2}}$ near their centres, which then decline exponentially in their outer parts. By modelling the HI morphology of the UDGs, we find a median inclination of $43^\circ$, in agreement with theoretical expectations for disc galaxies under UDG selection effects. Moreover, we place our UDGs in the $M_{\rm HI}-R_{\rm HI}$ and $M_{\rm HI}-R_{\rm 50,HI}$ mass-size relations, where $R_{\rm HI}$ is radius at which $\Sigma_{\rm HI}(R)=1\ M_\odot \rm{pc^{-2}}$, and $R_{\rm 50,HI}$ is the radius enclosing $50\%$ of $M_{\rm HI}$. While our UDGs lie within the scatter of the relations, they systematically fall on their upper side, being slightly (by $\sim 15-25\%$) more extended and of lower mean $\Sigma_{\rm HI}$ (by $\sim 25-35\%$) than average galaxies at similar $M_{\rm HI}$. Moreover, we find that $\Sigma_{\rm HI}(R/R_{\rm HI})$ and $M_{\rm HI}(<R)/M_{\rm HI}$ for UDGs follow an intermediate trend between late-type discs and early-type galaxies, with a large overlap with Sa galaxies.

2611.14639.title: Variations in the Extinction Curve at High Galactic Latitudes as seen by the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument

2611.14639.abstract: The dust extinction curve, characterized by the total-to-selective extinction ratio, $R(V)$, varies with grain size and composition. Accurate $R(V)$ values are crucial for dereddening astronomical colors and understanding the interstellar medium. We measure extinction toward stars with Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) spectroscopy using a machine-learning-based relative of the "pair method," matching reddened and unreddened stars. We use XGBoost to predict stars' intrinsic colors from their spectroscopic parameters ($T_\mathrm{eff}$, $\log g$, $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]$) and subtract them from observed colors to measure reddening in combinations of the $g$, $r$, $z$, $W1$, and $W2$ bands. This approach directly measures reddening, unlike the common thermal-emission-based method of Schlegel et al. (1998; SFD). The reddening is accurate to roughly 0.02 mag in $g-r$ and $r-z$. We develop a forward model to map $g-r$ and $g-W1$ reddenings to $R(V)$ and find significant variation in $R(V)$, with $\sigma_\mathrm{NMAD}(R(V)) = 0.23$, in dusty regions ($E(g-r) > 0.1$) at high Galactic latitudes observed by DESI. In this footprint, $R(V)$ is bimodal, with modes at 2.9 and 3.4, likely due to large-spatial-scale correlations in the shape of the extinction curve combined with the relatively small number of distinct sightlines with substantial reddening. We find no strong relationship between $R(V)$ and other tracers of the interstellar medium, such as thermal emission, dust temperature, spectral emissivity index $\beta$, and $H\alpha$. However, the error in the SFD-predicted extinction correlates well with $R(V)$, implying that a single optical reddening combined with the far-infrared dust brightness can predict variations in the extinction curve.

2611.14640.title: Tracing Galactic Dust Reddening with Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon Emission: SPHEREx Observations of the North Ecliptic Pole

figures.caption: Figure 1: SPHEREx 3.3 $\mu$m PAH emission in a $22^{\circ}$ by $22^{\circ}$ centered on the north ecliptic pole. The pixel scale is $6^{\prime\prime}.2$. Values are computed based on the method described in Section II.1 and many, though not all, of the point sources are removed in that procedure. For the purpose of visualization in this figure, we have used CloudClean.jl to inpaint masked pixels such as those vacated by point source masking [58].

Figure 2: 
Results of the galaxy density test for a suite of reddening maps at a common resolution of $16^{\prime}1$.
Only the region common to the coverage of all reddening maps is shown.
A small circular region ($0.86^{\circ}$ radius) in the lower right is also masked due to a high density of sources. This is likely spurious and may potentially be attributed to stars in a nearby galaxy that pass the ELG color cut.
The only clear large scale spatial feature is the underestimation of reddening seen toward the northeastern region of the maps.
This coincides with increased interstellar medium density in a region that is closer to the Galactic plane.
In the result for the HI reddening map, the hatched region indicates where $N_{\text{{H~I}}}>4\times 10^{20}$ cm-2.

The middle and the bottom panel show for stellar reddening maps (DESI, Gaia) and HI, respectively. The gray curve and band corresponds to the results for SFD and is shown in all three panels for comparison.
On the bottom panel, we also show the galaxy sample selected without correction for dust contamination (“None”). For better visibility, each spectrum is plotted with a slight offset in $\ell$.
No power spectrum corrected for dust contamination shows strong evidence of Galactic contamination. The spectrum of the uncorrected sample is nearly flat before aligning more closely with the corrected samples at higher $\ell$.

Figure 4: 
$\Delta E(B-V)$ vs. $q_{\rm PAH}$ for each reddening map.
The solid black line indicates the median values of nine equally sized bins.
The dashed black line indicates the corresponding median absolute deviations.
The Spearman correlation coefficient $r_{s}$ is also shown.
Estimating the uncertainty using bootstrapping, we find $\sigma_{r_{s}}\approx 0.04$.
For the HI reddening map, the gray number and trend indicates the relation when limited to only regions with $N_{\text{{H~I}}}<4\times 10^{20}$ cm-2 [42, i.e., the threshold from]. All reddening maps show weak correlations with PAH mass fraction ($|r_{s}|<0.1$) with the exception of the HI reddening map. However, this negative correlation largely disappears when applying the column density threshold ($r_{s}=-0.26\rightarrow-0.08$).

Figure 5: $\Delta E(B-V)$ vs. $f_{\rm PAH}$ for each reddening map.
Like Figure 4, the solid black line indicates the median values of nine equally sized bins, while the dashed black line indicates the corresponding median absolute deviations.
Estimating the uncertainty using bootstrapping, we find $\sigma_{r_{s}}\approx 0.04$.
For the HI reddening map, the gray number and trend indicates the relation when limited to only regions with $N_{\text{{H~I}}}<4\times 10^{20}$ cm-2 [42, i.e., the threshold from].
Compared to the minimal trends observed with $q_{\rm PAH}$ (Figure 4), the correlations for DESI, WISE, Gaia, and SPHEREx when compared against $f_{\rm PAH}$ are stronger. Again, we find that the negative correlation for the HI reddening map is substantially reduced when applying the column density threshold.

Figure 6: 
Comparison of dust reddening measured by SFD and SPHEREx in a $2^{\circ}$ by $2^{\circ}$ region within the NEP.

SPHEREx is shown with a pixel scale of $6".2$ in the middle.
On the right, for the purpose of visualization, we also show the SPHEREx $E(B-V)$ map where we have infilled masked pixels (typically point sources) using CloudClean.jl [58].

Figure 7: 
Ratio of $f_{\rm PAH}$/$q_{\rm PAH}$ against $f_{\rm PDR}$.
$f_{\rm PAH}$ and $q_{\rm PAH}$ remain proportional until enough WISE W3 emission is assigned to dust heated by intense radiation fields (i.e., larger values of $f_{\rm PDR}$) resulting in diverging predictions of PAH abundances. The dashed horizontal line at $\sim 0.045$ represents the typical $f_{\rm PAH}$/$q_{\rm PAH}$ ratio.

Figure 8: 
SPHEREx $\Delta E(B-V)$ vs. $q_{\rm PAH}$ and $\Delta E(B-V)$ vs. $f_{\rm PAH}$ correlations restricted to $f_{\rm PDR}<0.075$.
The result with the $f_{\rm PDR}$ cut is shown in black, while the correlation without the $f_{\rm PDR}$ cut is shown in gray.
Regardless of whether the comparison is against $q_{\rm PAH}$ or against $f_{\rm PAH}$, no change in correlation is observed when restricting to regions with minimal predicted $f_{\rm PDR}$.

Figure 9: 
SPHEREx $\Delta E(B-V)$ vs. $q_{\rm PAH}$ and $\Delta E(B-V)$ vs. $f_{\rm PAH}$ correlations without temperature correction.
The correlation without the temperature correction is shown in black while the correlation with the temperature correction (originally shown in Figure 4 and 5) is shown in gray.
With and without the temperature correction, correlations of the SPHEREx reddening map with $q_{\rm PAH}$ show minimal correlation change.
On the other hand, correlations of the SPHEREx reddening map with $f_{\rm PAH}$ show a reduction in correlation without a temperature correction ($r_{s}=0.13\rightarrow-0.08$).

2611.14640.abstract: We investigate the ability of SPHEREx observations of the $3.3$ $\mu$m polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) emission feature to trace Galactic dust reddening. Applying a spectral template-based method to SPHEREx data, we measure the strength of the $3.3$ $\mu$m PAH feature in each $6''.2$ pixel of a $22^{\circ}$ by $22^{\circ}$ region centered on the north ecliptic pole (NEP). We convert the PAH feature strength to reddening by applying a radiation field correction and a linear scale factor. The resulting $E(B-V)$ map is consistent with far-infrared, stellar, and HI-based reddening maps at arcminute scales, exhibiting a typical $E(B-V)$ difference of $\lesssim 7$ mmag. A galaxy count test finds that all reddening maps have a dispersion of $\approx11$ mmag in $E(B-V)$ relative to what would be needed to produce spatially uniform galaxy counts. While there is some evidence that reddening is overestimated by our map at high PAH abundances, this effect is smaller than the uncertainties on the applied radiation field corrections and limited to $\sim$10 mmag in the most extreme regions of the NEP. For a diffuse, high Galactic latitude region like the NEP and at the sensitivities of our validation metrics, the SPHEREx PAH-emission based reddening map matches the accuracy of existing reddening maps while being capable of accessing a higher angular resolution of $\sim6''$.

2611.14701.abstract: We investigate anomalously low-metallicity (ALM) star-forming regions in 11 galaxies from the Deciphering the Interplay between the Interstellar Medium, Stars, and the Circumgalactic Medium (DIISC) survey. We combine optical spectroscopy of 542 H$\alpha$-bright regions from MMT/Binospec with imaging from the Vatican Advanced Technology Telescope and H I 21 cm imaging from the Very Large Array. We find 75 ALM regions: 19 identified using deviations from each galaxy's radial metallicity gradient, 27 using the resolved mass--metallicity relation (rMZR), and 29 via both methods. Regions identified by both methods are metal-poor relative to their galactocentric positions and local stellar mass surface densities by $>$ 0.1 dex, making them the strongest candidates for localized metallicity dilution. We estimate accreted masses of $5.6<\log(M_{\rm acc}/{\rm M_\odot})<7.5$ for the 48 radial-gradient-selected regions, comparable to observed and simulated high-velocity cloud masses. We calculate a mean hydrogen accretion rate of $1.02\ {\rm M_\odot yr^{-1}}$ per galaxy, which is comparable to the mean star formation rate of the sample. The strongest ALM candidates lie within or near $R_{25}$, while rMZR-only regions dominate the outer population. We find no evidence that circumgalactic Ly$\alpha$ absorption along a single sightline traces disk chemical structure, as quantified by either the radial metallicity gradient or the fraction of radial-gradient-selected ALM regions. These results suggest that localized accretion of low-metallicity gas can sustain star formation in galaxies and demonstrate that ALM regions provide a spatially resolved indirect view of ongoing gas cycling.

2611.14734.abstract: Using the La Silla-QUEST and Gaia surveys, we identify 256 RR Lyrae stars (RRLS) in the Outer Virgo Overdensity (OVOD). These show that the OVOD has a signifcantly larger and more complex shape than previously recognized. The OVOD lies at an average distance of $\sim 85$ kpc, has a long dimension of $\sim 57^\circ$ ($\sim 85$ kpc), and a width that varies from $\sim 10^\circ $ ($\sim 15$ kpc) to $\sim 35^\circ $ ($\sim 50$ kpc) in a prominent bulge. Because it bends by $\sim 35^\circ$ from a great circle, it does not appear to be a stellar stream. The type ab RRLS (RRab) span a large range in period, with a mean of $0.59$ days, and only $19\pm 3 \%$ lie near the locus of Oosterhoff II variables in the Bailey diagram. The overall large number of RRLS along with a mean RRab metallicity ([Fe/H]) of -1.60 and $1 \sigma$ dispersion of 0.32, as inferred from the RRab periods, suggest that the OVOD progenitor was a large dwarf galaxy. The hypothesis that the OVOD may be a shell produced by the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger \citep{chandra2023} is supported by the $\sim 70^\circ$ angle that the southern extension of the OVOD makes with the orbits of red giants in its central part. The complex shape of the overall RRLS distribution, including a small north-south distance gradient, may also indicate, however, that we are seeing a blended, composite structure projected on the sky.

2611.14852.abstract: The velocity dispersion-size relation of molecular clouds, $\sigma_v = C\,(R/1\,{\rm pc})^{\gamma}$, has been reported with a power-law index ranging from $\gamma \approx$ 0.38 to 0.5 or higher, and a correspondingly varying normalization coefficient $C$, but the role of the intensity threshold in producing this scatter has not been quantitatively characterized. Using 4916 $^{13}$CO clouds identified with GDCluster (Liu & Du 2025) in the Milky Way Imaging Scroll Painting (MWISP) survey, we derive $\gamma$ and $C$ as functions of the intensity threshold $T_{\rm th}$. The index $\gamma$ increases monotonically with threshold, reaching a saturation value $\gamma_{\rm sat} \approx$ 0.56 for the full sample; splitting the sample by spiral arm gives higher values, $\gamma_{\rm sat} \approx$ 0.62 and 0.70. The normalization $C(T_{\rm th})$ declines monotonically, saturating at $C_{\rm sat} \approx$ 0.35 km/s and implying a surface density of ~46 Msun/pc^2 under a virial approximation. On the $\gamma(T_{\rm th})$ curve, $\gamma \approx$ 0.38 (Larson 1981) and $\gamma \approx$ 0.5 (Solomon et al. 1987) correspond to a low threshold ($T_{\rm th} \approx$ 1.2 K) and a near-saturation one (2.6 K), respectively, roughly consistent with the $^{13}$CO-equivalent boundary temperatures of these two studies. These two historically debated values, together with the broader $\gamma \approx$ 0.38-0.7 range reported in the literature, may largely reflect different positions along this single threshold-dependent curve and differences in sample composition. This threshold effect should therefore be considered when using Larson-type relations to assess the roles of turbulence and gravity. As an independent check, DBSCAN-identified $^{13}$CO and $^{12}$CO samples show the same monotonic trend in $\gamma$, though the curve shape differs quantitatively.

2611.15040.title: Moving Beyond the DRW Model: Learning Quasar Variability with Generative Models

figures.caption:
Figure 1: 
Illustration of null-hy$$$$$$p$$$$$$othesis mis-specification in a controlled synthetic example, based on 8,000 AR(2) light curves.
Top left: true joint distribution of AR(2) coefficients $(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})$ used to generate the light curves.
Top middle: estimated coefficient distribution obtained by fitting an AR(2) model to the simulated data, accurately recovering the true structure.
Top right: distribution of AR(1) coefficients obtained by fitting an incorrect AR(1) noise model to the same light curves, collapsing the correlated AR(2) variability into a single effective parameter.
Bottom left: p-value, i.e. the probability that the noise alone produces a Fourier amplitude at least as large as the value on the vertical axis, as a function of discrete frequency, for light curves generated from the true AR(2) model, shown on a logarithmic color scale.
Bottom middle: corresponding p-values obtained from the fitted AR(1) null model, on the same logarithmic scale.
In both panels, white pixels mark amplitudes that are not reached by any simulated noise realization at that frequency, so that the empirical p-value is zero (i.e. below the resolution set by the finite number of simulated light curves) and cannot be displayed on a logarithmic scale.
Bottom right: relative difference between the p-values computed under the correct AR(2) and the incorrect AR(1) null hypotheses, $\Delta p/p_{\mathrm{AR1}}=(p_{\mathrm{AR2}}-p_{\mathrm{AR1}})/p_{\mathrm{AR1}}$, shown on a symmetric logarithmic color scale (linear close to zero). Positive values indicate zones where the mis-specified AR(1) model gives a p-value that is too low, causing false positive detections, while negative values indicate zones where AR(1) gives a p-value that is too high, causing false negatives. Since $p_{\mathrm{AR2}}\geq 0$, negative values are bounded below by $-1$, which is approached where $p_{\mathrm{AR2}}\ll p_{\mathrm{AR1}}$, whereas positive values can greatly exceed unity where $p_{\mathrm{AR1}}$ is small. White pixels mark amplitudes at which $p_{\mathrm{AR1}}=0$, where the ratio is undefined.

Figure 2: Average PSDs of generated light curves compared to the target DRW PSD for both the DRW (Rayleigh) and Uniform-amplitude datasets.
Top row: Solid curves show the empirical average PSD computed from 3,000 generated samples; dashed curves show the analytic target DRW PSD used during dataset construction.
Bottom row: Absolute relative error between model and target PSD as a function of frequency.
Both datasets were constructed to have identical target PSDs but fundamentally different underlying Fourier-amplitude distributions (Rayleigh vs. Uniform).
The model recovers the same PSD accurately for both datasets, as shown by the close agreement across all frequencies and the small errors in the bottom panels.
This result is crucial: it establishes that the two datasets are indistinguishable at the level of the power spectrum.

Figure 3: 
Fourier-amplitude statistics for the Uniform-amplitude (ablation) dataset, standardized per frequency (centered and normalized to zero mean, unit variance).
Top row: Empirical distributions of standardized Fourier amplitudes at representative Fourier modes corresponding to approximately 1, 5, 22, and 102 oscillation cycles across the full generated light curve. Lower cycle modes correspond to lower temporal frequencies and longer timescale variability, while higher cycle modes correspond to shorter timescale fluctuations. The boxed annotation in each panel gives the raw mean $\mu_{k}$ and variance $\sigma_{k}^{2}$ of the amplitude at that bin. The distributions exhibit the characteristic bounded shape of the Uniform amplitude construction.
Bottom row: Quantile quantile (QQ) plots comparing generated amplitudes against reference distributions. A QQ plot tests whether two distributions match by comparing their quantiles: if they are identical, all points lie exactly on the identity line. Deviations from the line indicate differences in distributional shape or tails. Two comparisons are shown at each frequency: the orange line compares generated samples against a Uniform reference distribution, while the green line compares against a Rayleigh reference distribution. The close alignment of the orange line with the identity line across all frequencies demonstrates that the model successfully reproduces the Uniform amplitude distribution. This shows the model captures higher order ensemble level statistics beyond the power spectrum—specifically, the bounded tail structure characteristic of Uniform amplitudes.

Figure 4: 
Top row: Empirical distributions of standardized Fourier amplitudes at representative Fourier modes corresponding to approximately 1, 5, 22, and 102 oscillation cycles across the full generated light curve. Lower cycle modes correspond to lower temporal frequencies and longer timescale variability, while higher cycle modes correspond to shorter timescale fluctuations. The boxed annotation in each panel gives the raw mean $\mu_{k}$ and variance $\sigma_{k}^{2}$ of the amplitude at that bin. In contrast to Figure 3, the distributions exhibit the heavier, asymmetric tail characteristic of the Rayleigh distribution.
Bottom row: Quantile quantile (QQ) plots comparing generated amplitudes against reference distributions. Two comparisons are shown at each frequency: the green line compares generated samples against a Rayleigh reference distribution, while the orange line compares against a Uniform reference distribution. The strong alignment of the green line with the identity line across all frequencies and quantiles indicates that the model accurately reproduces the full Rayleigh ensemble distribution of the true DRW process. The clear deviation of the orange line from the identity line further confirms that the generated data have Rayleigh, not Uniform, tails. This demonstrates the model captures the heavy tail behavior and higher order statistical structure characteristic of DRW variability across multiple temporal scales.

Figure 5: Left: Joint distribution of AR(2) coefficients $(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})$ estimated from 4,000 light curves of the dataset that were not used in training, using the Yule-Walker equations.
Center: Model recovered coefficient density obtained by generating new light curves from the trained model, then estimating AR(2) coefficients from each generated sample using the Yule-Walker equations.
The Yule-Walker method is a standard technique for fitting AR(2) models to time series data by matching the empirical autocovariances.
Right: Difference between the data and recovered coefficient densities, where red indicates regions where the data distribution has more mass and blue indicates regions where the recovered distribution has more mass.
The close agreement between left and center panels demonstrates that the generative model successfully captures the statistical structure of the AR(2) population, as measured by the joint distribution of fitted coefficients $(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})$, despite never being explicitly told about the AR(2) structure during training.
This is quantified by a Wasserstein distance of $0.0168\pm 0.0011$ between the generated and data coefficient distributions, comparable to the distance of $0.0164\pm 0.0012$ between two independent samples of the data, indicating close agreement.

Figure 6: Recovery of AR(1) damping coefficients under conditional generation.
Each panel shows the estimated coefficient $\hat{\phi}$ as a function of the true coefficient $\phi$ of the conditioning light curve. The dashed line indicates perfect recovery. The shaded regions show the 25–75% and 5–95% quantile ranges of estimates, and the solid line shows the mean estimate, over 500 conditioning light curves per coefficient.
Left panel (Reference): For each conditioning light curve, the AR(1) coefficient is estimated, a new light curve is simulated with the estimated coefficient, and the coefficient is estimated again from the new light curve. This shows the intrinsic uncertainty when fitting AR(1) coefficients to finite length time series and simulating new realizations from the fitted model.
Right panel (Generative model): For each conditioning light curve, the generative model generates a new light curve, from which the coefficient is estimated. The mean estimates closely follow those of the reference across the full range of true coefficients, with a somewhat larger spread. The displayed model is the best of three independently trained models (see Appendix C.3).
All light curves have 256 data points.

Figure 7: Detection performance for periodic signal detection when the true stochastic varia$b$ility follows an AR(1) process.
Experimental setting: 1,000 synthetic AR(1) light curves were generated with damping coefficients $\phi$ uniformly distributed in $[0.1,0.9]$. Sinusoidal signals with randomly varying phase and amplitude were injected into half of them, with cycle ranges of 30 to 100 (one complete oscillation per 30–100 data points), signal to noise ratios between 0.5 and 0.8, and 100 Monte Carlo realizations simulated per light curve.
Detection procedure: The detection statistic is the maximum periodogram power $T(x)=\max_{k}|{\tilde{x}}_{k}|^{2}$. For each light curve, a p-value is computed by generating $N=100$ synthetic realizations from a noise model and computing $p=(b+1)/(N+1)$, where b is the number of realizations with $T(x_{\mathrm{null}})\geq T(x_{\mathrm{obs}})$. An ROC curve is constructed by varying the detection threshold and computing the true positive rate versus false positive rate across many light curves. The area under the ROC curve (AUC) measures performance: 1.0 indicates perfect separation between periodic and non-periodic signals, 0.5 indicates random guessing.
The generative model achieves an AUC of 0.9273, matching the fitted AR(1) reference (AUC 0.9042) and approaching the oracle bound (AUC 0.9646). The random-coefficient null, which does not use the observed light curve, achieves an AUC of 0.8291. The corresponding false-positive rates are given in Table 9 (Appendix D). This demonstrates the model successfully infers stochastic parameters from the observed signal and constructs an appropriate null distribution.

Figure 8: Distribution of p-values for the AR(1) experiment.
For each light curve, p-values were computed under different null hypotheses using the detection procedure from Fig. 7, here for a separate set of 400 light curves (200 with and 200 without an injected signal). Under the null hypothesis (no periodic signal), p-values should be uniformly distributed between 0 and 1, indicating the null model is properly calibrated. When a periodic signal is present, p-values should be concentrated near 0, indicating strong rejection of the null.
The AR(1) Estimated and Generative model methods both produce approximately uniform distributions under the null (negative) and p-values concentrated near 0 when signals are present (positive). The AR(1) Unestimated method shows degraded performance, with a broad distribution of p-values when signals are present. The Oracle method provides the best performance with strongest separation between null and signal-present cases. The generative model’s p-value distributions closely match the fitted AR(1) reference. The corresponding false-positive rates are given in Appendix D.

Figure 9: Detection performance for periodic signal detection when the true stochastic variability follows an AR(2) process.
Experimental setting: Synthetic AR(2) light curves were generated with coefficient pairs $(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})$ drawn from a correlated mixture of two Gaussian distributions (as in Section 4.2). Sinusoidal signals with randomly varying phase and amplitude were injected into 500 of 1,000 light curves, with cycle ranges of 30 to 80, signal to noise ratios between 0.8 and 1.2, and 100 Monte Carlo realizations simulated per light curve (300 for the AR(2) coefficient flow).
Detection procedure: Identical to Fig. 7: the detection statistic is the maximum periodogram power, p-values are computed from 100 synthetic null realizations, and ROC curves measure detection performance.
The AR(2) setting reveals a critical challenge with parametric null hypotheses: AR(2) processes are flexible enough to generate oscillatory fluctuations, so fitting AR(2) coefficients independently from each light curve causes the fitting procedure to absorb part of the injected sinusoidal signal as stochastic variability. This makes the fitted AR(2) null overly permissive (AUC 0.9180), degrading detection. The generative model achieves superior performance (AUC 0.9648, averaged over three independently trained models), approaching the oracle (AUC 0.9855), by learning the distribution of AR(2) coefficients across the training set and using this as a regularizing constraint: unlikely coefficient values are not favored merely because they can absorb a periodic component. The AR(2) coefficient flow, which explicitly combines the population distribution of coefficients with the observed light curve, performs similarly (AUC 0.9526). The mis-specified AR(1) null performs worst (AUC 0.8505). The corresponding false-positive rates are given in Table 10 (Appendix D). This demonstrates that data-driven null hypotheses can outperform parametric fitting when models are sufficiently flexible to absorb genuine signals.

Figure 10: Distribution of p-values for the AR(2) experiment.
For each light curve, p-values were computed under different null hypotheses using the detection procedure from Fig. 9. Ideally, p-values for signal-present cases should be concentrated near 0 (strong rejection of null), while p-values for null cases should be uniformly distributed between 0 and 1 (a properly calibrated null).
The AR(1) Misfit method fails catastrophically: p-values are concentrated near 0 for both null and signal-present cases, causing it to reject the null far too often. This produces widespread false positives (42% of the null cases at the 5% significance level).
The AR(2) Estimated method shows a uniform distribution for null cases (correct calibration) but the peak for signal-present cases is broad and not sharply concentrated near 0. This overlap between null and signal distributions causes both false positives and false negatives.
The AR(2) Oracle method approaches the ideal: p-values for signal-present cases form a sharp peak near 0, while null cases show a relatively uniform distribution. This provides good separation.
The Generative model (averaged over three independently trained models) achieves near-optimal performance: p-values for signal-present cases concentrate sharply near 0, while p-values for null cases are approximately uniform, as for the oracle. This provides good separation with a false-positive rate close to the nominal level (Appendix D). The AR(2) coefficient flow behaves similarly, with a somewhat broader peak for signal-present cases.

2611.15040.abstract: The optical continuum variability of quasars is often described by a damped random walk (DRW) model, with characteristic damping timescales $\tau_{\rm DRW}$ of hundreds of days and amplitudes $\sigma_{\rm DRW}$ of $\mathcal{O}(0.1)$ magnitudes. This model has been widely used as a null hypothesis to assess the significance of periodic signals in quasar light curves in the search for supermassive black hole binaries, the significance of extreme quasar variability like tidal disruption events (TDEs) and changing-look (CL) quasars, or to model time lags in reverberation mapping. However, the DRW model is known to be incomplete, and an incorrect null hypothesis can lead to biased significance estimates. We investigate the impact of such null-hypothesis mis-specification on the detection of periodic signals in synthetic quasar light curves and introduce the generative model Nullasar, capable of learning quasar variability directly from time-series data. We demonstrate that Nullasar, trained with flow matching, can learn delicate statistical properties of stochastic light-curve variability without explicitly assuming any noise model. We further demonstrate that Nullasar can learn correlated distributions of noise parameters and generate new light-curve realizations from a range of deviations from the Gaussian DRW noise model, approximating parametric descriptions of stochastic processes. When used as a null hypothesis for detecting periodic signals in synthetic light curves, Nullasar performs comparably to fitting the correct DRW model to each light curve, and outperforms parametric fitting when the variability follows a more flexible AR(2) model. Finally, we identify practical limitations, including sensitivity to contamination of the training set by non-null signals, and show that projecting the conditioning vector of the model onto its leading principal components largely mitigates it.

2611.15056.abstract: Gravitational microlensing in strongly lensed active galactic nuclei (AGNs) provides a powerful probe of accretion-disk structure and may offer a unique opportunity to identify sub-parsec supermassive binary black holes (SMBBHs) through distinctive signatures. Upcoming wide-field surveys are expected to discover a large sample of strongly lensed AGNs, a fraction of which may host SMBBHs detectable via microlensing. In this paper, we employ semi-analytic models to assess the detection prospects of sub-parsec SMBBHs in lensed AGNs, focusing on systems with resolvable multiple images suitable for microlensing analysis. Accounting for galaxy-scale strong-lensing statistics, and including the cluster-lensing contribution as an optimistic statistical extension, we estimate that up to approximately 87 such systems could be spatially resolved by individual upcoming surveys, including the Vera C. Rubin Observatory (Rubin), Euclid, China's Space Survey Telescope (CSST), and the Roman. For the Rubin WFD survey, we estimate that periodic oscillations in microlensing light curves could identify $\sim0.12-0.68$ short-period ($<5$\,yr) binaries, whereas diagnostics based on the reconstructed size-wavelength relation apply to a broader population, potentially identifying $\sim0.4-5.3$ systems, depending on the model assumptions. CSST, Euclid, and Roman may also reveal up to $10.6$, $8.9$, and $1.2$ systems exhibiting size-wavelength features, and $2.3$, $1.9$, $0.3$ systems showing periodic oscillations, which should be regarded as imaging-selected candidates whose microlensing-based identification requires adequate time-domain follow-up, including cadence, monitoring baseline, photometric precision, and reliable time-delay measurements. Our results show that strongly lensed AGNs provide a promising, though observationally demanding, pathway for finding candidate SMBBHs via microlensing.

2611.15166.abstract: We present the first reverberation mapping (RM) measurements in the COSMOS field included in the SDSS-V Black Hole Mapper Reverberation Mapping Project. Using $\sim$6 months of plate-based spectroscopy (from late 2020 to mid-2021) and accompanying ZTF+DECam \emph{gri}-band photometric light curves, we analyze the variability of over 250 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) out to $z \sim 3$. We successfully recover reliable $\lesssim$ 200d time lags for 22 AGNs ($z \lesssim 2.5$) in H$\alpha$, H$\beta$, MgII, or CIV, using a combination of multiple lag detection methods and significance tests. Our measurements are consistent with the radius-luminosity relations from recent large-scale RM programs, providing measured masses of $10^{7-9} M_{\odot}$ for these AGNs. These results and upcoming long-baseline SDSS-V spectroscopy lay the groundwork for large-sample AGN studies in conjunction with other facilities covering the COSMOS field, including the Vera C. Rubin Observatory and Roman Space Telescope.

2611.15272.abstract: Diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs) are absorption features of uncertain origin observed in the optical and near-infrared spectra of stars and galaxies. Although their correlation with dust extinction is well established, the physical conditions governing their strength across different interstellar medium (ISM) environments remain poorly understood. We investigate the environmental dependence of the DIB $\lambda5780$ using spatially resolved MaNGA spectroscopy for 837 nearby galaxies spanning a broad range of stellar masses, star-formation rates, and ISM properties. Stellar and nebular parameters are derived via spectral fitting, while DIB absorption is measured from high-signal-to-noise spatially binned residual spectra. We detect the DIB $\lambda5780$ in 159 galaxies and report the most distant spatially resolved DIB detection to date, at 232 Mpc. The DIB $\lambda5780$ equivalent width correlates positively with both stellar and gas-phase extinction. DIB $\lambda5780$ is preferentially detected in regions of high extinction, near- or super-solar metallicity ($12+\log({\rm O/H})\gtrsim8.5$), and moderate specific star-formation rates ($-10.5\lesssim\log({\rm sSFR}/{\rm yr}^{-1})\lesssim-9$). By contrast, it falls below our detection threshold in metal-poor or strongly ionized environments. It is rarely detected in regions with little or no recent star formation, with the few detections in such environments occurring primarily in regions driven by composite ionization. Our results indicate that DIB $\lambda5780$ is preferentially detected, within the sensitivity limits of the MaNGA data, in dust-rich, chemically evolved, and moderately ionized environments.

2611.15301.abstract: The Magellanic Stream (MS) is a gaseous structure extending over $150^\circ$ across the sky, likely formed through interactions between the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and SMC) as they fell into the Milky Way (MW). Its predicted stellar counterpart would provide a collisionless record of these interactions, but few candidate members have been identified. To expand this sample, we constructed a catalog of 87,763 distant K-giant candidates using DELVE DR2 and VHS DR5 photometry and Gaia DR3 astrometry, and analyzed VLT and Magellan spectra of 51 targets along the trailing MS. Combining radial velocities, spectrophotometric distances, and proper motions, we identify five new MS candidates at 58--95 kpc. Their metallicities are consistent with the outskirts of the SMC, while orbit integrations in a time-dependent MW--LMC--SMC potential support a possible Magellanic origin. Combined with previously identified candidates, these stars span a substantially broader range of Magellanic latitude than predicted by existing models, suggesting an extended debris field rather than a narrow stream. The candidates also lie predominantly closer than the simulated debris. More recent, less eccentric SMC orbits may help explain this distance discrepancy, although new simulations are required to test their implications for the stellar debris, along with larger spectroscopic samples.

2611.15303.abstract: The central regions of the Magellanic Clouds are crucial for understanding galaxy interactions and calibrating the cosmic distance scale, yet they remain observationally challenging due to extreme stellar crowding. We utilised deep VISTA observations (VMCDeep) to determine the highest-precision near-infrared Period-Luminosity (PL) and Period-Wesenheit (PW) relations to date for Classical Cepheids (delta Cep class, DCEPs) in the dense central regions of the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and SMC). We analysed J and Ks time-series data covering the central 1.77 deg^2 of each galaxy. Utilising approximately 40 epochs per filter and PSF-based photometry, we derived high-quality light curves for 573 and 2090 DCEPs in the LMC and SMC, respectively. We derived exceptionally precise PL and PW relations, exhibiting the lowest photometric dispersion published so far for the Magellanic Clouds. Fourier parameters calculated from the light curves indicate that pulsational models incorporating a mildly non-canonical mass-luminosity relation and a mixing-length parameter of alpha = 1.7 best reproduce the observations. Age derivations confirm a bimodal star formation history in the SMC centre. Crucially, we discovered a striking line-of-sight spatial dichotomy within the young SMC DCEP population (t < 116 Myr), which is bifurcated into two distinct structures separated by ~4 kpc. This provides independent stellar evidence tracing a recent direct collision with the LMC. Finally, by unifying fundamental and first-overtone pulsators, we derived a highly constrained relative distance between the Clouds. Comparing this to detached eclipsing binary distances, our data suggest a moderate metallicity correction for the Leavitt Law with gamma ~ -0.2 mag/dex.

2611.15355.abstract: Radial surface brightness profiles (SBPs) and color gradients are useful tools for studying galaxy structure, formation, and evolution. While it is usually assumed that they are primarily driven by stellar properties, such as mass, age or metallicity, their dependence on 3D dust attenuation is not fully understood or accounted for. We analyze how 3D dust attenuation affects galaxy observations by hindering the estimation of intrinsic properties. We examine dust-induced shifts in surface brightness and color. Using SKIRT radiative transfer models, we simulated simple Sérsic galaxies, with spherically-symmetric stellar densities, constant stellar-to-dust ratios, and a spatially constant spectral energy distribution (SED). We find that attenuated SBPs differ significantly from dust-free profiles, particularly in the central galaxy regions. These differences become more pronounced at bluer wavelengths and for higher core dust densities, leading to variations in the fitted Sérsic index of up to ~25%. This can lead to incorrect conclusions about the intrinsic stellar distribution and mimic a central mass deficit. For galaxies with very centrally-dense dust distributions, a core-Sérsic model results in a better fit of the attenuated SBP. For dust masses as low as ~2*10^6 $M_{\odot}$, dust-induced negative color gradients reach the same order of magnitude as those commonly observed in galaxies, which a dust-screen fails to account for. This occurs even for a spatially invariant SED and can lead to wrong conclusions about intrinsic stellar populations and related astrophysical questions, such as their formation histories or the mechanisms of inside-out star formation quenching. A full 3D approach is necessary to properly model attenuation effects, which, if not accounted for, can bias inferences made about stellar populations, their evolutionary histories, and spatial distributions.

2611.15528.abstract: In the standard cosmological model, the distribution of cold dark matter (CDM) can be reshaped by baryonic processes through gravity, as gas outflows alter the central potential and transform steep cusps into nearly constant-density cores. However, such feedback-generated cores are generally expected to have sizes comparable to the visible stellar body of a galaxy. Here we report the discovery of an exceptionally extended dark matter core in a nearby gas-rich dwarf galaxy UGCA 320. We combine high-resolution MUSE H$\alpha$ kinematics in the inner region with high-, medium-, and low-resolution MeerKAT HI observations from the MHONGOOSE survey tracing the galaxy out to large radii. After accounting for an additional non-circular kinematic component identified in the central HI spectra, we construct an extended rotation curve to constrain the dark matter distribution. The resulting rotation curve is poorly reproduced by a cuspy Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) halo but well described by cored pseudo-isothermal (ISO) and Burkert halo models. Consistently, a fit with a generalized NFW model yields an inner density slope of $\gamma=0.36\pm0.12$, quantitatively supporting a shallow central density profile. The best-fit ISO model gives a dark matter core radius of $7.62\pm0.80$ kpc, approximately four times the stellar half-light radius and substantially larger than typically found in dwarf galaxies. We investigate the main systematic uncertainties and find that the resulting core radii remain large, all lying within 3$\sigma$ of the fiducial fit. The exceptionally large core in UGCA 320 may pose a challenge to the standard CDM paradigm. While its properties are broadly consistent with self-interacting dark matter (SIDM), they may be difficult to reconcile with warm and fuzzy dark matter models, as well as the stellar feedback-driven core formation scenario.

2611.15556.abstract: Stellar populations in the central regions of disc galaxies provide key constraints on their formation and secular evolution. We investigate the properties of young stellar populations in the centres of nearby barred galaxies from the TIMER survey, using four stellar population models, two based on empirical (MILES, X-Shooter) and two on theoretical (Starburst99, HR-pyPopStar) stellar libraries, complemented by independent gas-phase metallicities from emission-line diagnostics. The inferred stellar metallicities depend strongly on the adopted model. Measured as the 5th-to-95th percentile spread across the three galaxies analysed in detail, the empirical libraries recover variations of 1.11 and 0.98 dex, whereas the theoretical ones return 0.40 and 0.49 dex; the gas in the same regions spans 0.49 dex. Gas metallicities are indeed lower in the central star-forming regions, but the amplitude of that depression (about 0.3 dex in NGC 1097) exceeds what bar-driven inflow of disc gas can account for, given typical abundance gradients in literature. The age-metallicity relations consistently reveal two distinct components: an older population consistent with a self-enrichment scenario, and a younger population formed from gas inflows with a different chemical enrichment history. The empirical libraries produce a monotonic decline of metallicities from old to young populations, which would require a sustained inflow of metal-poor gas outpacing its own enrichment. The theoretical libraries instead recover a young component whose metallicity departs from the older populations only at the most recent ages and by a few tenths of a dex, compatible with a single dilution episode. Our results demonstrate that model choice critically affects inferred metallicities, with empirical stellar libraries recovering age-metallicity relations that demand physical conditions the gas measurements cannot sustain.

2611.15560.abstract: Measuring the mass of the Milky Way is essential for understanding galaxy formation and evolution, characterizing the Galactic potential and assembly history, and probing the nature of dark matter. We derive the enclosed mass profile of the Milky Way out to Galactocentric distances of $\sim80\,\mathrm{kpc}$ using two halo tracers with full 3D kinematics: RR Lyraes (RRLs) and blue horizontal-branch stars (BHBs). Our sample consists of 7,550 RRLs and 8,230 BHBs constructed from the Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST), the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), and the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), spanning Galactocentric distances from $10$ to $100\,\mathrm{kpc}$. We estimate the enclosed mass using two independent methods: the spherical Jeans equation and the tracer mass estimator (TME). The two tracers yield consistent results, with $M(<81.7\,\mathrm{kpc}) = (4.76 \pm 0.23)\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ from RRLs and $M(<82.8\,\mathrm{kpc}) = (4.66 \pm 0.35)\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ from BHBs. Adopting an NFW profile to extrapolate the enclosed mass beyond the outermost radius probed by our tracers, we infer virial masses of $M_{200} = 8.12^{+0.72}_{-0.65}\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ from RRLs and $M_{200} = 8.13^{+0.78}_{-0.67}\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ from BHBs. We further validate our methodology using mock RRL and BHB samples constructed from two Auriga halos, finding that the inferred masses are underestimated by $15.5\%\pm2.8\%$ for RRLs and $11.9\%\pm3.4\%$ for BHBs, respectively. After correcting for these systematic errors, the Milky Way virial masses are $M_{200} = 9.79^{+0.93}_{-0.84}\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ from RRLs and $M_{200} = 9.24^{+0.95}_{-0.84}\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ from BHBs.

2611.15581.abstract: In this work we present a new approach to derive HII region metal abundances based on sulfur emission lines. We select M101 as benchmark galaxy to test our new methodology along the wide metallicity gradient of this huge face-on star-forming spiral. Based on previous studies, we compile a sample of 151 HII regions and compare their properties base on the galaxy radial profile. The new methodology is based on the derivation of the electron temperature of the double ionised sulfur, either by the direct measurement of the [SIII] auroral line or, at supersolar metalicities, from the $SO_{23}$ parameter. This new indirect method is able to extend the abundance gradient up to the very centre of the M101 galaxy (0.04 $R_e$). This new methodology mitigates systematic biases in direct abundance determinations based on auroral lines, while opening up new opportunities to improve commonly used strong line abundance calibrations in the intermediate to high metallicity regime.

2611.15850.abstract: The traditional method to measure Type-1 Active Galactic Nuclei central black hole masses ($M_{BH}$) is the reverberation mapping (RM) technique. Motivated by the desire to find a less observationally expensive method (than RM) to estimate $M_{BH}$, we have explored a purported correlation between X-ray luminosity and $M_{BH}$. For this we have compiled a sample of 35 AGN with RM $M_{BH}$ estimates that were detected in the eROSITA All-Sky Survey public data release. Using a sample that is larger than that of J. A. Mayers et al. 2018 and has a cleaner selection function, we confirm their XMM-Newton based result of a positive correlation. However, the scatter on the scaling relation remains too high ($\sigma_\mathrm{int}=0.50^{+0.08}_{-0.06}$) to make this a practical method to predict $M_{BH}$ for a given X-ray detected Type-1 AGN. That said, our findings can be used to improve mock X-ray skies generated from large volume hydrodynamical cosmological simulations. Such mocks are a necessary ingredient for cluster cosmology and preparation for future missions such as NewAthena.

2611.15855.abstract: The dynamical evolution of globular clusters is significantly influenced by the multiscale structure introduced by the presence of multiple stellar populations. In this study, we investigate the long-term dynamical evolution of the stellar mass function (MF) within globular clusters hosting two stellar populations using a suite of Monte Carlo simulations run with the MOCCA code. Dynamical processes including two-body relaxation, mass segregation, and tidal stripping result in distinct radial profiles describing the variation with distance from the cluster's center of the stellar MF slope within the first population (P1), the second population (P2), and the cluster as a whole. We show that these radial profiles are well described by a broken power law with a knee located slightly interior to the half-mass radius, a feature partially driven by the multiscale structure of the multiple populations. In both 3D and 2D projected coordinates, we explore several characteristic clustercentric distances within the profile, including those where the local MF slope matches the global value of the present-day MF slope and the initial mass function (IMF) slope, and we examine how these positions evolve with the cluster's dynamical age. Our results highlight how the initially more centrally concentrated P2 drives a steeper radial gradient and a steeper MF slope in the outer regions, which subsequently affects the global cluster values. Motivated by recent observational studies suggesting that a bottom-light IMF may better describe massive globular clusters, as well as measurements of a flatter P2 MF slope in the outer regions of 47 Tucanae, we additionally explore a three-parameter bottom-light IMF and a simulation in which the P1 IMF differs from the P2 IMF, with the P2 IMF flatter than that of the P1 in the lower mass range.

2611.15866.abstract: Omega Centauri ($\omega$ Cen; NGC 5139), the likely stripped nucleus of a dwarf galaxy accreted by the Milky Way, is one of the few galactic nuclei resolvable into individual stars. Because of its long relaxation time, the kinematics of its stars may still retain memory of how this nucleus formed. We combine HST proper motions and MUSE line-of-sight velocities from the oMEGACat survey to compare populations defined by abundance variations (the chromosome map), metallicity, and age within the half-light radius. The chromosome-map division separates two dynamically distinct components. The primordial stars have a flattened dispersion field, with kinematic ellipticity $\epsilon \approx 0.7$ ($\sigma_{\rm minor} / \sigma_{\rm major} \approx 0.8$), which we recover independently in the line-of-sight velocities and the proper motions. The enriched stars are consistent with $\epsilon=0$ in the line-of-sight velocities and are no more flattened than the full sample in the proper motions, and the two components show no strong difference in rotation. Metallicity bins show no comparable structure, because each bin mixes stars from both components, and the age-metallicity sample covers only the cluster core, where it cannot test for the flattening. The present-day central concentration of the most enriched (P2) stars suggests that they formed more centrally concentrated than the primordial stars, independent of assembly scenario. These results favor a picture in which the primordial stars retain the flattened orbital structure of the progenitor, while the enriched stars fell inward as dense clumps or formed in compact, centrally concentrated starbursts.

2611.15877.abstract: The Euclid mission is revolutionising the study of strong gravitational lenses by providing high-resolution imaging over an unprecedented survey area, increasing the number of known lenses by two orders of magnitude compared to previous surveys. Characterising this sample of lens-galaxies requires accurate measurements of their physical properties. However, standard catalogue photometry often blends the light from the foreground lens and the lensed background source, limiting the reliability of derived galaxy parameters. We present a homogeneous catalogue of photometric redshifts and physical properties for 9538 galaxy-scale strong lenses identified in Euclid's DR1 strong-lens sample. We use deblended multiwavelength photometry obtained from the lens modelling of Euclid and ground-based images with PyAutoLens. The photometric redshifts of the lens galaxies are estimated using the template-fitting code Phosphoros. The stellar masses, SFRs, stellar ages, and metallicities are inferred through SED fitting with Prospector, adopting a flexible non-parametric SFH and a Salpeter IMF. The robustness of the inferred parameters is assessed through comparisons with spectroscopic redshifts and external galaxy surveys. The sample of lenses spans a broad redshift range of $0.13\lesssim z_{\rm phot} \lesssim 1.98$, with a median $z_{\rm phot} = 0.68^{+0.33}_{-0.29}$. The sample is dominated by massive quiescent galaxies with a $M_\ast$ range $[10^{10},\,10^{12.1}]\,M_\odot$ and a median $\log_{10}(M_\ast/M_\odot) = 11.39^{+0.29}_{-0.33}$. This catalogue represents one of the first large-scale characterisations of strong-lens galaxies in the Euclid era. By combining deblended photometry with homogeneous photometric redshift and SED-fitting analyses, it provides a foundation for studies of galaxy evolution, lens-galaxy scaling relations, and the connection between stellar and total mass in strong lenses.

2611.15880.abstract: The Magellanic Clouds benefit from a wealth of data across the electromagnetic spectrum, but extracting extragalactic sources from these crowded fields is a less than straightforward endeavour. We used an unsupervised machine learning algorithm (t-distributed stochastic neighbourhood embedding; t-SNE) to classify 6,652 and 1,356 sources in the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, respectively, that were detected in the VISTA Survey of the Magellanic Clouds (VMC) and the Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) survey with the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP). Multi-wavelength photometry and colours from optical to radio were used as features to cluster similar sources together in 2D space on a t-SNE map. We used previously classified sources to separate the clusters into five classes: AGN, low-redshift galaxies, blazars, dusty stellar objects (e.g. young stellar objects, planetary nebulæ etc) and high proper-motion stars. Previous photometric classifications from the literature match with specific clusters identified, as well as provide insight on areas of the t-SNE map for which there are no previous classifications. This work shows that the combination of unsupervised machine learning with photometry from optical to radio has proven adept at separating the stellar from the extragalactic, and the AGN from the galaxies. Our associated new spectroscopy with SALT includes new discoveries of AGN up to redshift 3.3 and Magellanic emission-line objects.

2611.15883.abstract: We present 15 072 high-confidence strong lens candidates in Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1), spanning 2000 deg$^2$. These comprise 6073 grade A ('sure lens') and 8999 grade B ('probable lens') systems, which we publish alongside a further 9010 grade C ('possible lens') candidates. With more high-confidence candidates than all previous catalogues combined, this sample establishes a large, homogeneous data set of galaxy-scale strong lenses with high-resolution imaging, transforming strong lensing from a field of rare discoveries to a robust statistical tool for astrophysics and cosmology. Of the roughly 900 million sources in DR1, we searched the 68 million passing our catalogue selection using a bespoke discovery pipeline that synthesises scores from five machine-learning models with visual classifications from around 7000 citizen scientists and 67 strong lensing experts. Beyond classical Einstein rings, our catalogue includes 84 candidate double-source-plane lenses and over 1000 candidate disc lenses, two exotic classes with few previously known examples, as well as several hundred candidate lensed AGN and quasars. We deliver automated lens models for the combined grade A+B systems, and photometric redshifts and stellar population properties for the deflector galaxies, providing immediate science-ready data products. We find that the majority of the deflector galaxies are massive and quiescent, with stellar masses of $\log_{10}(M_\ast /M_\odot) = 11.39^{+0.29}_{-0.33}$ (Salpeter initial mass function; 16th-84th percentile range). The deflector galaxies span a range of photometric redshifts ($z=0.68 ^{+0.33}_{-0.29}$), extending to higher redshifts than previous ground-based lens samples, and the lenses have a typical Einstein radius of $0.85 ^{+0.44}_{-0.24}$ arcsec. Extrapolating by area, we expect over 100 000 high-confidence strong lens candidates in the Euclid Wide Survey.

2611.15884.abstract: We present a statistical analysis of ionized gas outflows in a large sample of low-mass ($\mathrm{log(M_{*}/M_{\odot})\lesssim10}$) galaxies at $z<0.45$ from the first data release of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI DR1). Using [OIII] and H$\alpha$ emission lines, we identify $\sim5800$ dwarf galaxies with robust signatures of ionized outflows. Most are star-forming systems above the star-forming main sequence, with a smaller fraction of composites and AGN hosts. The derived mass-loading factors span $\eta=0.001-1$, with a median $\eta\sim0.01$, consistent with previous studies at similar stellar masses. These values are $1$--$2$ dex lower than predicted by cosmological simulations, suggesting that the ionized phase traces only a minor fraction of the total outflow mass. Outflow velocities are sufficient to enrich the circumgalactic medium in $\gtrsim80\%$ of cases, while escape into the intergalactic medium appears efficient mainly in composite and AGN hosts. We find that mass-loading factors decrease with stellar mass, broadly reproducing simulated trends despite the normalization offset. Comparing individual detections with stacked spectra of the general low-mass star-forming population, we find systematically lower mass-loading factors in the stacks, although the difference decreases toward larger offsets above the star-forming main sequence. Together with a positive correlation between mass-loading factor and specific star-formation rate, this suggests that enhanced star formation and burstiness regulate feedback efficiency and shape galactic winds. Our results highlight the role of ionized outflows in the baryon cycle of low-mass galaxies and the need for multiphase studies to fully understand feedback in galaxy evolution.

2611.15886.abstract: We present the method used to identify the $15\,000$ high-grade galaxy-galaxy strong lens candidates in Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Given that lenses are intrinsically rare systems and the DR1 data set is vast, this lens search was conducted in a number of stages: a catalogue-level cut; a machine-learning and ensemble search; a two-stage citizen-science search, and finally grading of lens candidates by strong lens researchers. In this paper, we describe each search stage and their respective results. This search was enabled by the automated classification of over 68 million objects by neural networks, more than 4.5 million classifications of $300\,000$ objects by citizen-scientist volunteers, and the inspection of over $30\,000$ objects by strong lens researchers. We find this multi-stage approach helps maximise the number of lenses identified, while minimising inspection requirements of both citizen scientists and strong lens researchers. We measure a completeness in our comprehensive search of $0.73_{-0.15}^{+0.08}$ to grade A ('definite') systems and $0.34_{-0.06}^{+0.05}$ to grade A+B ('definite' + 'probable') systems. Our search therefore identifies the majority of the definitive strong lens systems in the DR1 area with the remainder likely to be fainter or more ambiguous cases. We find that researcher grading remains subjective; in this work we implement calibration to account for biases of individual inspectors and highlight the benefit of lens modelling (ECLIPSE-C) in determining the nature of a lens candidate. This paper forms part of the ECLIPSE series, here focussing on the discovery pipeline used to identify lens candidates in Euclid DR1; an overview of the lenses discovered is presented in ECLIPSE-A.

2611.15888.abstract: Galaxy-scale strong lenses provide precise measurements of galaxy mass distributions, magnified views of distant galaxies, and a competitive cosmological probe. Historically, such studies have been limited to hundreds of lenses, with automated modelling methods proving difficult to scale. We present automated lens modelling of 15 072 strong-lens candidates from Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1), over an order of magnitude larger than any previously modelled sample. Using PyAutoLens-JAX, we perform three fits with multi-Gaussian expansion (MGE), pixelised, and Sérsic representations of the source, adopting an isothermal ellipsoid mass model with external shear. These fits provide foreground lens-light subtraction, adaptive Delaunay source reconstructions, and deblended photometry. More than 20 expert inspectors visually assess the resulting models, and each model is assigned the classification on which at least 75% of its inspectors agree. Of the 6073 grade A (secure) lens candidates, inspectors classify 4098 (67.5%) as successfully modelled, 580 (9.6%) as failures, 317 (5.2%) as multi-galaxy lenses, 15 (0.2%) as double-source-plane lenses, and 7 (0.1%) as unsure if lens, while 1032 (17.0%) reach no consensus and 24 (0.4%) have incomplete models. For the 8999 grade B (probable) candidates, the modelling success rate falls to 43.1%, primarily reflecting an increase in cases without consensus (37.6%), rather than a comparable increase in agreed failures (12.9%). Successfully modelled grade A and B systems have a median effective Einstein radius of 0.85 arcsec and a median total $I_E$-band source magnification of 8.1. We publicly release the successful lens models, their inferred properties, and magnified-source reconstructions through the ECLIPSE catalogue, demonstrating automated modelling at Euclid sample sizes and enabling population-level strong-lensing science.

2611.15915.abstract: Population III (PopIII) stars are the first generation of metal-free stars, thought to form in minihalos ($M_\mathrm{halo} \sim10^5-10^6\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$) at Cosmic Dawn ($z\gtrsim15$) before largely giving way to Population II stars formed from the newly enriched medium. Simulations show, however, that PopIII stars may continue forming at low rates through the Epoch of Reionization (EoR, $z \sim 6 - 10$), due to the inhomogeneous enrichment of the Universe. Nonetheless, significant uncertainty remains on the rates and typical environments of late PopIII formation. We use the CampFIRE-6k cosmological zoom-in simulation to examine PopIII star formation history and environments through $z\sim6$. We find that PopIII stars form at a near constant rate ($\sim 10^{-3.5} ~\mathrm{M_{\odot}\,yr^{-1}\,cMpc ^{-3}}$) through $z=6$, including within atomic-cooling halos ($M_\mathrm{halo}\sim 10^7-10^8\,\mathrm{M_\odot}$) at late times.

2611.15931.title: Anatomy of LyC Escape in MEGATRON: Connecting Feedback Physics to Demographics, Leakage Timescales, and Explorations of ISM Density as a Tracer of Escape Fraction

figures.caption:
Figure 1: An IGM-scale view of the efficient star formation MEGATRON simulation at redshift $\bm{z\sim 11}$.
A variety of projections through the MEGATRON simulation are shown. These include intrinsic properties such as the dark matter density field (light purple), gas density (dark purple), temperature (orange), and LyC flux (white), as well as direct predictions of $\rm H\beta$ (blue) and $\rm[O~{\small III}]~\lambda 5007$ (red) emission lines. A composite of these features is also shown in the top panel, inheriting the same colours.

Figure 2: Reionization history and UV number counts.
Redshift evolution of the IGM ionized fraction ($x_{\rm HII}$, top) till the end of the simulation at $z\sim 8.5$ as well as the measured distribution of UV magnitudes (bottom) among snapshots below redshift $z\lesssim 16$ for each MEGATRON simulation. We include observed UVLFs renormalised to the high $\epsilon_{\rm ff}$, HN simulation at $\rm M_{\rm UV}=-19$ for comparison. While the high $\epsilon_{\rm ff}$, HN simulation features the fewest galaxies, it produces the fastest reionization history. The opposite is true for the efficient star formation simulation.

Figure 3: Galactic contributions to Reionization.
Cumulative fractions of the total escaping LyC photons released by galaxies below redshift $z\leq 14$ as a function of UV magnitude (top) and halo virial mass (bottom) for each MEGATRON simulation. Magnitudes and masses corresponding to $50\$$ of the contributed LyC photons are denoted by dashed vertical lines. Different feedback models lead to changes in the relative importance of UV bright/faint galaxies, while leaving the dependence on halo mass less impacted.

Figure 4: Escape fraction, ionising production efficiency, and escaping ionising luminosity population demographics.
We show distributions for $\xi_{\rm ion}$ (both the intrinsic value alongside that inferred from $\rm H\alpha$), $f_{\rm esc}$, and $\dot{N}_{\rm ion,esc}$ for all galaxies with $\rm M_{\rm UV}\leq-13$ across all four MEGATRON simulations. Changes to star formation/feedback physics modify escape fraction distributions while leaving $\xi_{\rm ion}({\rm H\alpha})$ largely unchanged. However, the mapping to $\dot{N}_{\rm ion,esc}$ is non-trivial. For example, while the bursty star formation model produces the largest number density of strong leakers ($f_{\rm esc}\gtrsim 30\%$), the ionizing output of these galaxies is systematically lower than those of the high $\epsilon_{\rm ff}$, HN simulation.

Figure 5: Ionizing Luminosity as a function of Magnitude.
We show running medians for the escaping ionizing luminosity of galaxies as a function of $\rm M_{\rm UV}$ for galaxies below redshift $z\leq 16$ across all four MEGATRON simulations. Both the normalisation and scatter (shown by shaded areas which mark the $16^{\rm th}$ and $84^{\rm th}$ percentiles) in this relation are sensitive to feedback physics and can be conditional on $\rm M_{\rm UV}$. Among very faint galaxies ($\rm M_{\rm UV}\sim-10$), there is a boost due to the ionizing luminosity of Population III stars. As a comparison, we show the running median from the THESAN-ZOOM simulation (Summerfield et al., 2026).

Figure 6: Time-evolution of LyC production and escape.
We show running medians of $f_{\rm esc}$, $\dot{N}_{\rm ion,int}$, and $\dot{N}_{\rm ion,esc}$ as a function of the ionizing luminosity-weighted mean stellar age for galaxies in each MEGATRON simulation with $\rm M_{\rm UV}\leq-17$ (solid) and $-17\leq\rm M_{\rm UV}\leq-13$ (dashed). Changes to feedback physics (e.g., burstier star formation, stronger early feedback, and preferentially forming stars in low-density gas) all act to shorten the time delay between a particular starburst and the onset of effective leakage. As the intrinsic ionizing luminosity decreases with time, a shorter gap will lead to more effective leakage. To highlight this, we include a dashed vertical line at $\sim 3.5~{\rm Myr}$, at which point the first Type II SNe begin. Interestingly, the UV-bright population is capable of releasing similar numbers of ionizing photons, while the output of UV-faint galaxies is strongly dependent on feedback.

Figure 7: Typical SFHs of LyC-leaking galaxies.
We show median SFHs of galaxies with $\rm M_{\rm UV}\leq-15$ in the bursty star formation simulation, stacked as a function of $f_{\rm esc}$ (top) and $f_{\rm esc}\xi_{\rm ion}^{\rm int}$ (bottom). These have been smoothed with a Gaussian kernel of standard deviation $\sim 1~\rm Myr$ and renormalised at the present day. Rapidly rising SFHs are emblematic of non-leakers, while on average, LyC-leaking systems appear to be in the post-starburst phase due to the need for a strong feedback episode to clear channels through the neutral ISM.

Figure 7: Typical SFHs of LyC-leaking galaxies.
We show median SFHs of galaxies with $\rm M_{\rm UV}\leq-15$ in the bursty star formation simulation, stacked as a function of $f_{\rm esc}$ (top) and $f_{\rm esc}\xi_{\rm ion}^{\rm int}$ (bottom). These have been smoothed with a Gaussian kernel of standard deviation $\sim 1~\rm Myr$ and renormalised at the present day. Rapidly rising SFHs are emblematic of non-leakers, while on average, LyC-leaking systems appear to be in the post-starburst phase due to the need for a strong feedback episode to clear channels through the neutral ISM.

Figure 8: Multi-phase ISM structure of non-leaking galaxies compared to intermediate and strong LyC leakers.
In each panel, we show mass-weighed density-temperature phase diagrams of all gas in the ISM of a mass-matched ($10^{6}\leq{\rm M_{*}/M_{\odot}\leq 10^{6.5}}$) sample of galaxies. Each column corresponds to a stack of galaxies with LyC escape fractions within a specific range (larger $f_{\rm esc}$ from left to right). Similarly, each row corresponds to the relevant stack for each MEGATRON simulation. While the intrinsic ISM structure is different for each simulation as a function of changes to star-formation/feedback physics, the mechanisms that drive the production of escape channels are unchanged. Strong photoionization feedback is present in intermediate leakers ($1\%\leq f_{\rm esc}\leq 10\%$), strong leakers ($10\%\leq f_{\rm esc}\leq 50\%$) display a combination of photoionization and SNe feedback, while the cold/dense ISM of extreme leakers ($f_{\rm esc}\geq 50\%$) is almost completely disrupted.

Figure 9: Density/temperature structure of LyC leakers.
We show ISM gas mass fractions as a function of density (left) and temperature (right) for each MEGATRON simulation (rows). Each line is computed by integrating the relevant phase diagram of Figure 8. The ISM of galaxies with larger LyC escape fractions feature progressively less dense/cold gas and significantly more hot gas. Similarly, the ratio of peaks at $\sim 10^{4}~{\rm K}$ and $\sim 10^{4.5}~{\rm K}$ is sensitive to $f_{\rm esc}$, indicating the presence of strong photoionization feedback.

2611.15931.abstract: Constraining the Lyman Continuum (LyC) escape fraction ($f_{\rm esc}$) of high-redshift galaxies is essential to connect the abundant populations revealed by \textit{JWST} to cosmic reionization. We investigate this interplay using {\small MEGATRON}, a suite of zoom simulations with detailed radiation/chemistry and varied feedback prescriptions. We find that feedback physics simultaneously regulates UV source counts, LyC escape fractions, and escaping ionizing luminosities ($\dot{N}_{\rm ion,esc}$), producing different reionization histories. These differences are governed by the delay between a starburst and LyC escape: efficient early feedback and lower-density environments enable photons to escape while pre-supernovae stellar populations remain strongly ionizing. Consequently, models that produce fewer UV-bright galaxies yield earlier LyC escape and reionize sooner than models with more abundant UV sources and delayed LyC emission. Furthermore, UV-faint galaxies follow a common physical sequence in ISM structure with increasing $f_{\rm esc}$ irrespective of feedback physics: stronger leakers ($1\%\leq f_{\rm esc}\leq 50\%$) exhibit evidence of strong photoionization and SNe feedback alongside post-starburst star formation histories, while extreme leakers ($f_{\rm esc}\geq 50\%$) have also cleared their cold/dense ISM. We find that electron densities inferred from the $\rm [O\,{II}]\,\lambda\lambda3727$ doublet are a candidate diagnostic of $f_{\rm esc}$, with lower densities around $\rm H~{\small II}$ regions selecting stronger leakers. Moreover, this density can trace the early evolution of $f_{\rm esc}$, whereas UV slope-based calibrations over-predict $\dot{N}_{\rm ion,esc}$ for individual young galaxies by up to two orders of magnitude. Overall, the delayed duty cycle of LyC leakage must be accounted for when UV source counts are interpreted in the context of reionization.

2611.15948.abstract: We derive the mass-loss rates of asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars in the isolated dwarf irregular galaxy NGC 6822 using SEDust, an automated pipeline that fits spectral energy distributions (SEDs) to estimate stellar mass-loss and dust-production rates. The total mass-loss rate of the AGB population is $(3.7 \pm 1.1) \times 10^{-3} M_\odot\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. For a gas-to-dust ratio of 200, this corresponds to a dust injection rate of $2.0 \times 10^{-5} M_\odot\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. If sustained over 10 Gyr, this rate would yield approximately $2 \times 10^{5} M_\odot$ of dust, which is lower than the dust mass of $2.7 \times 10^{5} M_\odot$ estimated from Herschel observations. AGB stars alone therefore cannot account for the present-day dust reservoir of NGC 6822, and additional sources or processes, such as dust growth in the interstellar medium, are required.

2611.16025.abstract: We searched within the first data release of the Euclid Wide Survey (~1900 deg^2) for resolved stellar systems between distances from 10 kpc and several Mpc, using an isochrone filtering technique. We detect 15 systems that have never been resolved into stars before. Five are new discoveries, three in the Milky Way halo and two beyond the Local Group. The remaining ten are dwarf galaxies that were previously catalogued as unresolved sources in shallower ground-based surveys and lack reliable distance measures. We measured distance moduli for all 15 systems, and half-light radii, ellipticities, position angles, absolute magnitudes, and stellar masses for 14 of them. In the Milky Way halo, Ursa Minor II, at ~20 kpc, has Mv ~ +2.0 and a stellar mass of ~40 Msun, and is one of the least luminous stellar systems known. Fornax 7 is located near the tidal limit of the Fornax dwarf spheroidal galaxy and may be physically associated with it. Eridanus V lies at ~165 kpc and has a stellar mass of ~550 Msun, which places it in the region of the size-luminosity plane where globular clusters and ultra-faint dwarf galaxies overlap. Beyond the Local Group, the 12 dwarf galaxies lie at distances of 3--5.5 Mpc. Three of them reach or exceed a mean surface brightness within the half-light radius of mu_V~28 mag/arcsec^2, a regime in which almost no galaxies at these distances were previously known. Ten of them are candidate members of the M81 group: eight have three-dimensional distances from M81 smaller than or comparable to the radius of its zero-velocity surface, and two lie close to the peripheral member NGC 4236, one of which is a candidate satellite of this galaxy. These results demonstrate Euclid's transformative potential for low-surface-brightness science, enabling the study of an unprecedented range of environments from the MW halo out to the Local Volume within a single, homogeneous survey.

2611.16109.abstract: Understanding the intrinsic 3D shapes of galaxies provides crucial insights into their formation and evolution, but determining these from projections remains challenging. We apply a Bayesian inference framework to optical images of galaxies from the Euclid Data Release 1, leveraging its large sample size to test the scalability and robustness of this methodology. Applying Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) sampling to Sérsic axis ratios and effective radii, we constrain the population-level mean 3D ellipticity, triaxiality, and size, together with their covariances for $40\,864\,304$ star-forming galaxies with stellar masses $M_\ast=10^{9}$--$10^{10.5}M_\odot$ at redshifts $0<z<1.2$. Our sample size exceeds previous shape inference studies by factors of $440$--$52\,800$ relative to early observations by JWST, and factors of $440$--$17\,600$ relative to legacy observations from HST in overlapping mass-redshift bins, enabling finer binning alongside improved statistical constraints on shape evolution. We additionally include over 9 million galaxies at $z<0.5$, a regime historically limited by sample size in previous shape inference studies. We recover key evolutionary trends identified in previous smaller-sample studies. We find high ellipticities ($\mu_E \sim 0.600$--$0.821$) across all bins, indicating that the underlying 3D shape distributions are statistically dominated by flattened geometries. Most notably, we recover the decline of the prolate fraction towards $z=0$ at low masses ($M_\ast=10^{9}$--$10^{9.5}M_\odot$) reported by previous studies. This trend is seen consistently in comparable analyses of independent data sets spanning different depths and resolution regimes, showing that it is not an artefact of small-sample statistics, suggesting it may be a genuine feature of galaxy evolution. We also identify future methodological improvements for subsequent Euclid data releases.
